items.title: I found dead weight inside an AI model in 3D
items.summary: Two heads in this model do nothing for us, and they're bigger than the one we actually use. Every block here is one real tensor of GLiNER, at its real size: 419 of them, nearly half a billion weights. A post goes in at the top and a decision comes out at the bottom. The unused heads are the span and count heads, far bigger than the classifier head we do use. Strip them out and it still makes every decision. The I-shape in the middle is a 24-layer transformer. items.title: NVIDIA cuPhoton Brings Real-Time Black Hole Science to GPUs
items.summary: NVIDIA cuPhoton moves the scientific data pipeline onto GPUs, helping researchers study black holes as events unfold. - Eight radio observatories worked together as a virtual telescope the size of Earth to capture the first image of a black hole in the M87 galaxy - cuPhoton streams only the data needed for black hole jets and overlaps loading with signal processing, reconstruction, analysis and visualization, all of which AI agents can run - It speeds up data loading by up to 3,700x and correlation by up to 460x, scaling across multi-node systems powered by the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform - Data can now be acquired at rates up to 345 GHz, cuPhoton reduces months of compute to minutes and help resolve the light rings around black hole Learn More: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/high-performance-computing/ai-for-science/cuphoton/

items.title: Real-Time Discovery Starts With NVIDIA DAQIRI
items.summary: Every discovery begins with a signal. NVIDIA DAQIRI connects high-bandwidth instrument data to accelerated computing, so AI can process live sensor streams while an experiment or industrial process is still underway. Instead of capturing data, writing it to disk, and analyzing it later, workflows can sense, reason, and respond in real time. - Streams hundreds to thousands of gigabits of instrument data per second into GPU memory - Berkeley Lab’s Molecular Foundry uses DAQIRI to stream over 500 Gb/s from a new camera, delivering results during the experiment - Enables live scan analysis, telescope signal characterization, experiment guidance, and synchronized interactive digital twins Learn More: https://developer.nvidia.com/daqiri

items.title: What Happens When Engineers Stop Reading Their Own Code?
items.summary: In this episode, we sit down with Matt Carey and Scott Crooks, engineers at Cloudflare and Miro, to look at how two very different companies are building their own AI software factories, and what happens to engineering when the code mostly writes and reviews itself. We start with the AI gateway: why a model call is no longer simple when the same model is served across multiple regions, multiple clouds, and direct from the provider, and how Miro pools rate limits and data residency rules (like EU-only models for German customers) into a single routing layer that also powers Miro’s Sidekicks. Matt walks through Cloudflare’s agent stack, from the AI gateway and Agents SDK to Flue, a JavaScript agent framework from the makers of Astro, and Cloudflare OS, an open source agent office suite he even runs at home for grocery shopping. The heart of the conversation is code review. Matt describes what he calls the best AI code reviewer he’s ever used, built on Flue and powered by an internal engineering codex written only for agents. Scott breaks down Miro’s three-layer setup, including Easel, a bot that reads production logs overnight and opens fix PRs before anyone wakes up, and explains why only about half of those PRs get merged, and how that signal is fed back to teach the system what people care about. Along the way, we cover agent experience as a new discipline, how open source maintainers are handling a flood of cheap AI pull requests, Astro reaching zero open issues, when companies should open source internal tools and how to retire them gracefully, plus a few hot takes on chocolate and nuts. We close on the rise of the “scholarly engineer,” and why understanding ideas may matter more than reading every line of code. items.title: Forecasting, Time Series & Anomaly Detection: Predicting What Comes Next
items.summary: Some of the most valuable questions in any organization are about time. What will demand look like next quarter? When will this equipment need maintenance? Terms covered: - Forecasting: using historical data to predict future values, accounting for seasonality, trends, external events and interdependencies that traditional statistical methods struggle with at scale - Time Series Models: built for sequential, time-ordered data, designed to detect the temporal patterns that a standard model treating each data point independently would miss - Anomaly Detection: flagging when reality diverges from what is expected. A spike that signals fraud, a temperature reading before equipment failure, a behavior pattern suggesting a breach. Forecasting tells you what is coming. Time series models give you the accuracy to trust it.
